Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# Mercury Crater-naming Contest Winners Announced

*Published on 29 April 2015*

![Mercury's full disk with five newly named craters labeled: Carolan, Enheduanna, Kulthum, and two others indicated by lines pointing to detailed surface images.](/images/PR/PR2015/newly-named-mercury-craters-header.jpg?version=DB618BAB)

![Mercury's full disk with five newly named craters labeled: Carolan, Enheduanna, Kulthum, and two others indicated by lines pointing to detailed surface images.](/images/PR/PR2015/newly-named-mercury-craters-header.jpg?version=DB618BAB)

The MESSENGER Education and Public Outreach (EPO) Team has announced the winners from its competition to name five impact craters on Mercury after artists. Winners were selected by the IAU from 3600 submitted names.

The [MESSENGER](http://messenger.jhuapl.edu/) Education and Public Outreach (EPO) Team, coordinated through the [Carnegie Institution for Science](http://carnegiescience.edu/), has announced the winners from its competition to name five impact craters on Mercury after artists. Entries had to be submitted by 15 January 2015, and the International Astronomical Union (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](http://www.iau.org/science/scientific_bodies/working_groups/98/) made the selections from a total of 3600 submissions, and a semifinal round of 17 names. The newly selected crater names are Carolan, Enheduanna, Karsh, Kulthum, and Rivera.

Under IAU rules, all new craters on Mercury must be named after an artist, composer, or writer who was famous for more than 50 years and has been dead for more than three years.

Turlough O'Carolan (Carolan) was an Irish composer during the late 16th and early 17th centuries; Enheduanna, an Akkadian princess who lived in the Sumerian city of Ur in ancient Mesopotamia (modern Iraq and Kuwait), and is regarded by many scholars as the earliest known author and poet; Yousuf Karsh was an Armenian–Canadian and one of the greatest portrait photographers of the 20th century; Umm Kulthum was an Egyptian singer, songwriter, and film actress active between the 1920s and 1970s; and Diego Rivera was a prominent Mexican painter and muralist between the 1920s and 1950s.

NASA’s *MESSENGER* spacecraft has been in orbit about Mercury since March 2011 and its mission is due to finally end when it impacts into the planet tomorrow. The *MESSENGER* spacecraft has far surpassed expectations in both the duration of its mission and in the quantity and quality of data it has provided; the goal of the craft was to take 2500 images of the planet, but it has returned more than 250 000. The EPO team organised the crater-naming competition to celebrate the mission’s achievements.

The winning suggestions came from many different countries. Carolan was suggested by Fergal Donnelly (Belguim), Joseph Brusseau (USA), and Deane Morrison (USA). Enheduanna was submitted by Gagan Toor (India). Karsh was submitted by Elizabeth Freeman Rosenzweig (USA). Kulthum was suggested by Molouk Ba-Isa (Saudi Arabia), Riana Rakotoarimanana (Switzerland), Yehya Hassouna (USA), David Suttles (USA), Thorayya Said Giovannelli (USA), and Matt Giovannelli (USA). Rivera was suggested by Ricardo Martinez (Mexico), Rebecca Hare (USA), Arturo Gutierrez (Mexico), and José Martinez (USA).

Founded in 1919, the IAU is the world's largest professional body for astronomers.

The Carnegie Institution for Science is a private, nonprofit organisation headquartered in Washington, D.C., with six research departments throughout the U.S. Since its founding in 1902, the Carnegie Institution has been a pioneering force in basic scientific research. Carnegie scientists are leaders in plant biology, genetics, developmental biology, astronomy, materials science, global ecology, and Earth and planetary science.

MESSENGER (MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging) is a NASA-sponsored scientific investigation of the planet Mercury and the first space mission designed to orbit the planet closest to the Sun. The *MESSENGER* spacecraft was launched on 3 August 2004, and entered orbit about Mercury on 18 March 2011 (UTC), to begin its primary mission — a year-long study of its target planet. *MESSENGER*’s first extended mission began on 18 March 2012, and ended one year later. *MESSENGER* is now in a second extended mission, which is scheduled to conclude in April 2015. Sean C. Solomon, the Director of Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, leads the mission as Principal Investigator. The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory built and operates the *MESSENGER* spacecraft and manages this Discovery-class mission for NASA.

method.instructions: Define both predicates precisely, including entity unit, eligible subtypes, exclusions and effective dates. Start sequentially with one X search, one Y search and one conjunction search. Maintain deduplicated dual frontiers and a ledger of canonical identities, aliases, evidence for each predicate, unresolved facts and estimated next-action cost. Group pending candidates into meaningful cohorts by their discovery source or eligibility subtype; do not invent arbitrary cohorts when none are useful. Separate evidence-backed near-intersections from speculative candidates that satisfy only one predicate. Resolve near-intersections first. For a speculative cohort, check at most three diverse candidates before committing more spend, and limit each dispatch to 10% of the initial budget; a single necessary check may exceed that cap if affordable. Inspect returned evidence before dispatching another sample. If a sample yields no verified addition or materially improved evidence, park that cohort and test another partition or the reverse frontier. No-hit candidates remain unresolved, not rejected. Revisit a parked cohort when new evidence, an alias or a demonstrably different source gives a better resolution path; a failed sample never proves the cohort empty. Expand productive cohorts in similarly small rounds, comparing verified additions and evidence progress per actual spend against discovery alternatives. Retain one neglected-cohort or reverse-frontier probe after two productive rounds so early samples do not permanently starve rare subtypes. After two discovery queries add no plausible identities, change source, subtype or frontier rather than paraphrasing the conjunction. Reuse established facts and never repeat settled checks. Keep at least 35% of initial budget for verification and evidence resolution, and stop discovery earlier if the promising pending queue requires it. End with identity, scope and date checks; submit only individually supported intersections and do not infer completeness from sampling or search saturation.

Escalate only individual promising unresolved cases to Exa alone with 4 results after a cheap check or targeted fetch fails; never escalate a whole cohort because one member is ambiguous. Following baseline sampling and genuine Parallel stagnation, allow one Exa discovery probe on the weaker frontier if the resolution reserve remains intact; retain Exa discovery only for useful incremental evidence or identities. method.fetch_policy: Cache facts and URLs. Fetch when source content can resolve a material identity or predicate uncertainty, or a discovered list supplies several plausible candidates.
